A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same research work, despite the model renaming and substantive revisions. Their text, equations, tables, figures, and appendices support reliable comparison, including matching material moved between the main text and appendices.

before.justification: v1 reports original synthetic latent-reconstruction experiments and natural-scene/movie decoding results from four mice, with latent-space analyses.

after.justification: v2 reports original results on non-temporal and temporal synthetic data, neural decoding from five mice, and extensive component and sensitivity analyses.

M1.justification: Section 3.2 replaces positive-only cosine-distance alignment with NT-Xent contrastive learning using negative samples and adds L2 regularization of the prior mean and log-variance. These substantially revise training. The recurrent content/style architecture and content-swapping operation remain under the new name TiDeSPL-VAE.

E1.justification: v2 adds Lorenz-generated temporal neural data and a time-shuffled counterpart alongside the retained non-temporal synthetic and natural-scene/movie datasets. This introduces ground-truth dynamical-trajectory recovery, directly testing temporal capabilities that v1's synthetic coverage did not address.

E2.justification: Corresponding benchmark comparisons retain beta-VAE, LFADS, pi-VAE, Swap-VAE, and CEBRA, with PCA retained for neural decoding. Moving synthetic baseline visualizations into Appendix F does not remove comparators. The new Lorenz benchmark uses the existing comparator set.

E3.justification: Reported training budgets change from 1,000 synthetic and 200 neural-data epochs to 20,000 synthetic, 5,000 scene, and 20,000 movie iterations; their equivalence cannot be established. v2 adds Lorenz and sensitivity-testing protocols and increases the mouse sample from four to five. Appendix neuron counts identify v1's Mice 3–4 as v2's Mice 4–5.

E4.justification: v2 adds temporal shuffling, loss-component removals, independent-prior and recurrent-module comparisons, and latent-dimension/input-neuron sensitivity studies (Section 4.4 and Appendix H). Content/style decoding and movie-window sensitivity already existed in v1; the former is revised and extended to movies.

E5.justification: v2 specifies five random-initialization runs and standard errors for the new temporal synthetic experiment (Table 1). Retained comparisons continue ten-run reporting. This adds a different run-count specification without establishing increased repetition of existing experiments.

E6.justification: Neural scores are extensively revised: the proposed model's Mouse 1 scene accuracy changes from 80.8% to 96.4%, and Mouse 2 movie accuracy from 49.01% to 65.38%, under revised training (v1 Tables 1–2; v2 Tables 2–3). Lorenz, fifth-mouse, and ablation results are added. On the newly included Mouse 3 movie task, CEBRA scores 61.01%, exceeding TiDeSPL-VAE's 59.88%.

T1.justification: Appendix B adds an explicit mathematical definition of the NT-Xent objective in Equation 18. The existing temporal ELBO factorization and derivation, Poisson loss, and Gaussian KL derivation in Equations 9–17 remain substantively unchanged.

C1.justification: The central claims about self-supervised sequential representations, visual decoding, and temporal structure remain. The abstract and introduction now explicitly characterize content as stimulus-driven activity and style as internal-state dynamics, refining the claimed biological meaning of the learned spaces.

C2.justification: v2 develops biological explanations for the content/style split and asymmetric recurrent updates. It also interprets the new controls as evidence concerning negative samples, temporal priors, recurrent choices, dimensional saturation, and neuron contributions. The existing limitation concerning variability across mice and trials remains.

D1.justification: Appendix C supplies a Lorenz generation and training recipe, including three latent variables, 30 neurons, five conditions with 20 trials each, and 1 ms sampling. Section 4.3 newly specifies a neuron-balance threshold. Backbone and A100 disclosures remain unchanged; Appendix E largely relocates existing baseline-input instructions.

R1.justification: The introduction substantially revises literature coverage toward behavior-informed LVMs and visual decoding, adding works such as targeted neural dynamical modeling and multimodal Gaussian-process VAEs while removing several classical dimensionality-reduction references. Positioning shifts from an explicit Swap-VAE extension toward a biologically motivated split sequential LVM, while retaining acknowledgment of Swap-VAE.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, related work, and method motivation are extensively rewritten, with revised title and terminology. Neural experiments are reorganized into combined setup/results subsections; synthetic-generation and baseline-input descriptions move into appendices, and a dedicated ablation section is introduced.

P2.justification: v2 adds temporal-benchmark and ablation tables plus sensitivity plots. Figure 2 is condensed with baseline panels moved to Appendix F; the content/style bar analysis becomes tables. Latent visualizations are redrawn and rearranged, and neural-data tables and appendix visualizations expand to accommodate the fifth mouse.

improvement.justification: v1 supported temporal and component claims mainly through neural decoding, visualizations, and non-temporal synthetic data. v2 adds ground-truth temporal recovery with a shuffling control and extensive component/sensitivity ablations (Sections 4.2/4.4 and Appendix H), substantially strengthening validation. These gains outweigh a new inconsistency between Equation 18's style variables and Section 3.2's content-variable description. Revised training budgets also mean higher reported scores alone cannot establish a method improvement.
